[1] (Innovative technologies to manage aflatoxins in foods and feeds and th, p.9) 5. Conclusions This review has focused on different scientiﬁc research results regarding AF control in food and feeds at pre- and post-harvest levels. It is clear that high AF levels pose human health risks and also represent a barrier to expand trade in both domestic and international contexts. Overall, it is necessary to tackle existing global food insecurity issues by adopting and implementing cutting-edge technologies. Biocontrol technologies, in conjunction with other aﬂatoxin-management tools such as sorting technologies, storage, irradiation, ozone fumigation, chemical and biological control along with improved packaging materials have the potential to link farmers to markets, enhance international trade, improve health conditions of people and animals, and increase food safety and security. However, multidisciplinary and comprehensive research is still required to assess the potential beneﬁts of these technologies. Overall, AF control interventions should be considered in order to improve food security, raise public health awareness, increase economic beneﬁts, and reduce related costs for all actors in commodity value chains.
[2] (Innovative technologies to manage aflatoxins in foods and feeds and th, p.7) 3. Beneﬁts of innovative management Many innovative management strategies that can potentially reduce AF contamination in food and feed chains have been identiﬁed by this review. These strategies have the potential to mitigate adverse effects of AF contamination on food security, public health, and economic development. An understanding of these beneﬁts can motivate policy makers and value chain actors to explore effective ways of managing AFs during pre- and post-production processes.
[3] (Innovative technologies to manage aflatoxins in foods and feeds and th, p.1) Aﬂatoxins are mainly produced by certain strains of Aspergillus ﬂavus, which are found in diverse agricultural crops. In many lower-income countries, aﬂatoxins pose serious public health issues since the occurrence of these toxins can be considerably common and even extreme. Aﬂatoxins can negatively affect health of livestock and poultry due to contaminated feeds. Additionally, they signiﬁcantly limit the development of international trade as a result of strict regulation in high-value markets. Due to their high stability, aﬂatoxins are not only a problem during cropping, but also during storage, transport, processing, and handling steps. Consequently, innovative evidence-based technologies are urgently required to minimize aﬂatoxin exposure. Thus far, biological control has been developed as the most innovative potential technology of controlling aﬂatoxin contamination in crops, which uses competitive exclusion of toxigenic strains by non-toxigenic ones. This technology is commercially applied in groundnuts maize, cottonseed, and pistachios during pre-harvest stages. Some other effective technologies such as irradiation, ozone fumigation, chemical and biological control agents, and improved packaging materials can also minimize post-harvest aﬂatoxins contamination in agricultural products. However, integrated adoption of these pre- and post-harvest technologies is still required for sustainable solutions to reduce aﬂatoxins contamination, which enhances food security, alleviates malnutrition, and strengthens economic sustainability. © 2017 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Ltd. This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
Why is it important to adopt both pre-harvest and post-harvest technologies to reduce aﬂatoxin contamination?

Integrated adoption of pre- and post-harvest technologies is required to reduce aflatoxin contamination sustainably. [3] Aflatoxins can negatively affect the health of livestock and poultry due to contaminated feeds. [3] Biological control using competitive exclusion of toxigenic strains by non-toxigenic ones is a potential technology for controlling aflatoxin contamination in crops. [3] Aflatoxins are a problem during storage, transport, processing, and handling steps. [3]

[1] (Guide to Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Surveillance, control, and product, p.23) 3.2.1 Spread of BBTV by the banana aphid • Banana aphids are small, oval-shaped insects (2–3 mm) that range in color from reddish-brown to nearly black (Fig. 17). They are present in all banana-growing regions worldwide. When they feed on an infected banana plant, they can pick up the BBTV from the plant’s sap and transmit it via their saliva to healthy plants (Fig. 18).
[2] (Guide to Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Surveillance, control, and product, p.64) Viruliferous means carrying and capable of transmitting a virus. In the case of the banana aphid and BBTV, a viruliferous banana aphid carries the BBTV and can transmit it to a banana plant when it feeds on the plant sap. Virus indexing. In the context of plant viruses, virus indexing is the process of testing plants for the presence of specific viruses to ensure they are free from infection. Virus indexing is particularly important in agriculture and horticulture, where virus-free plants are essential for maintaining healthy crops and preventing the spread of diseases. Common methods of virus indexing include: • Serological tests, such as ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay), which detect viral proteins. Molecular tests, such as PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction), which detect viral genetic material. Virus transmission. In the context of BBTD, virus transmission refers to the movement of BBTV from an infected banana plant to a healthy one. This occurs primarily through banana aphids (Pentalonia nigronervosa), which acquire the virus by feeding on the sap of an infected plant and then spread it by feeding on healthy plants. BBTV can also spread through infected planting materials, such as suckers taken from an infected mother plant. Water sucker. A water sucker of banana is a weak vegetative shoot with broad leaves and poor attachment to the mother corm, which generally develops into an unproductive banana plant. Water suckers are not recommended for fruit production.
[3] (Strategies for bean production: An agricultural extension manual for t, p.76) Photo 31. Beans affected by common mosaic virus. Source: Boaz Waswa/CIAT These two diseases are primarily spread through seeds. The viruses causing the disease increase in the presence of weed hosts. However, transmission from plant to plant could occur mechanically, through pollen, and most commonly the aphids that are vectors of the diseases. The diseases spread in warm and medium rainfall conditions that promote the aphid vector populations. Symptoms of attack include: ▶ Wrinkled or rolling leaves of light-green or yellow and dark-green patterns. ▶ Mottling, curling, and malformation of bean leaves. ▶ General stunting of the plant. The most effective management practice for controlling the diseases is planting disease-free bean seeds. Other management practices involve: ▶ Planting resistant bean varieties. ▶ Removing and destroying diseased plants. ▶ Carrying out timely planting to help escape the period of high aphid populations. ▶ Destroying other legumes and weed hosts before planting or during the cropping period. ▶ Applying insecticides such as Lava, Dudu, and Rocket, which manage aphids.
Which insecticides are recommended for managing aphids that transmit bean diseases?

Planting disease-free bean seeds is the most effective management practice for controlling the diseases. [3] Destroying other legumes and weed hosts before planting or during the cropping period helps control the diseases. [3]

[2] (Strategies for bean production: An agricultural extension manual for t, p.49) 2.3.1 Contour bunds These are small molds of soil, typically up to 50 cm high, heaped across a slope to act as a barrier for holding runoff. Use contour bunds when the amount of runoff you intend to control can be managed through infiltration. This is because contour bunds help to promote controlled water infiltration in bean fields. The interval of the contour bunds depends on the slope of your land. Bean fields located on steep slopes require bunds at closer intervals. To reinforce the bunds, plant strips of agroforestry trees such as Grevillea and forage such as Napier grass (Photo 16). Photo 16. A sloping field with a Napier grass strip planted to reinforce a contour bund. Source: Open AI (2025) An agricultural extension manual for the eastern region of the Democratic Republic of Congo
[3] (Strategies for bean production: An agricultural extension manual for t, p.21) Proper management of bean fields is important to maintain appropriate levels of soil moisture for an extended period. Choose appropriate soil and water conservation strategies to control waterlogging and flooding. In situ water harvesting and soil drainage improvement help in decreasing runoff by promoting storage of more water in the soil. Too little moisture, even for short periods within a season, diminishes the ability of bean plants to take up nutrients and affects the functioning of soil organisms. The following practices maintain appropriate soil moisture: ▶ Increasing soil organic matter ▶ Maximizing soil cover through cultivating cover crops or retaining crop residues ▶ Increasing plant diversity on the farm ▶ Decreasing soil disturbance ▶ Using ripping to break hardpans/compaction layers ▶ Constructing contour bunds, furrows, and ridges to retain or drain off excess water

Plant strips of agroforestry trees to reinforce contour bunds. [2] Bean fields on steep slopes require contour bunds at closer intervals. [2]

The spatial distribution of daily crop water requirement (mm day-1) of the selected legume crops at the late-season growth stage. The Potential , spatial patterns of the Seasonal Soil Water Satisfaction Index (SI) reveal marked differences in the degree to which residual soil moisture meets crop water requirements across legume crops and spatial locations (Figure 6). High SI values (0.8–1.0), indicating no to mild water stress, are predominantly concentrated in the southern and south-western highlands for most crops, reflecting favorable post-rainfall soil moisture conditions and relatively reliable satisfaction of crop evapotranspiration demand. Moderate SI values (0.6–0.8) dominate large portions of the central and southern areas, suggesting recurring but manageable water limitations during the growing season. In contrast, extensive areas in the eastern and southeastern lowlands exhibit low SI values (<0.6), indicative of severe seasonal water stress where residual soil moisture is insufficient to meet crop water demand.

Continuous occurrence of MLN in the MLN hotspots of Uganda is linked to the continuous presence of these perennial weeds and cultivated crops grown in association with maize each season which can act as sources of inoculum for the main virus driving the MLN epidemic in Uganda. The prevalence of these perennial weeds in major maize growing agro ecological zones is likely to indicate a major source of the MLN viruses carried through the dry season when the maize crop has been harvested. In addition, the presence of cultivated crops and weeds plants as alternate hosts, presents the need to identify MLN non hosts in cultivated crops for crop rotation and early weeding to reduce on MLN virus inoculum in the agro ecosystem. Failure of farmers to adopt these management strategies may result in a constant increase in MLN disease inoculum in the MLN hotspot areas and contribute to early infection of most maize plants with resultant losses in yields that are severe.

BBTV can also spread through infected planting materials, such as suckers taken from an infected mother plant. Water sucker. A water sucker of banana is a weak vegetative shoot with broad leaves and poor attachment to the mother corm, which generally develops into an unproductive banana plant. Introduction Cassava (Manihot esculenta Crantz) is one of the most important staple food crops in many countries of sub-Saharan Africa due its underground storability and flexibility in harvesting, which ensures a year-round food supply [1–3]. However, its production is hampered by a diverse set of biotic constraints, among which the most economically important and dangerous is cassava brown streak disease (CBSD) [1,4,5]. CBSD is a viral disease that has been known for many years in coastal East Africa [6,7] and is a key biotic constraint threatening cassava production, its quality, and quantity [4,8,9]. Two cassava brown streak ipomoviruses (CBSIs), named Cassava brown streak virus (CBSV) and Ugandan cassava brown streak virus (UCBSV), cause CBSD [10,11] and heavily constrain the food and income security of millions of rural farmers in eastern, central, and southern Africa [1,4,12]. The impact of CBSD is devastating [12–14] in eastern and central Africa, where the disease is now established and from which it is spreading to neighbouring countries [1,4,15,16]. There are several different symptoms in the CBSD syndrome [13]. On leaves, the disease appears as a feathery chlorosis on either side along secondary and tertiary veins [6,17]. There are several variants of this symptom, depending on cultivar, crop age, and weather conditions [17,18]. Characteristic CBSD foliar symptoms normally occur only on mature lower leaves, while young expanding leaves are symptomless [19]. On the stem, elongated necrotic brown lesions appear, resulting in dieback, although these symptoms only occur in highly sensitive varieties infected [17,18,20]. The most important and economically damaging symptoms are the yellow or brown corky necrotic root rot that occurs in the storage roots in the starch-bearing tissues [1,6,17]. Consequently, this renders them unsuitable for consumption or marketing, thereby affecting the livelihoods of poor farmers [4,17,21]. CBSD causes yield loss in susceptible varieties by reducing growth, as well as through the induction of root necrosis [1,17,22,23]. Root necrosis increases in severity as plants age. Where this damage is severe, the tuberous roots become inedible and unusable, resulting in their disposal as waste [4,18,21]. Root necrosis typically begins to develop around 9 MAP and gradually increases in severity up to and beyond normal harvesting time [12,17,22,23]. Losses due to CBSD have been estimated at US$ 75–100 million annually [8,13,24]. Originally confined to East Africa, CBSD started to spread in central Africa in the 2000s [25,26]. Recent regional cassava disease and pest surveys have shown that CBSD is spreading rapidly in eastern DRC and now poses a significant threat to cassava production in the country [4,9,27]. In the late 1990s and early 2000s in the DRC, the annual cassava production, which was around 20 million tonnes, declined drastically to 14 million tonnes due to severe CMD associated with East African cassava mosaic virus-Uganda (EACMV-Ug) [28–30]. This was successfully addressed through the deployment and large-scale multiplication of CMD-resistant varieties [31]. More recently, there has been an increasing focus on controlling cassava virus diseases through the improvement of seed systems [1,12,32]. These approaches emphasize establishing centres for producing virus-free planting material and managing seed quality in extensive seed propagation networks using seed quality certification based on phytosanitary controls [1,15,33]. However, the development of a sustainable cassava seed system in the DRC is facing multiple constraints, with one of the most significant being the scarcity of disease-free cassava planting material due to the degeneration of existing plant material, which is susceptible to CBSD [4,9,34].

The most devastating diseases are cassava mosaic disease (CMD) and cassava brown streak disease (CBSD). [1] Cassava mosaic disease (CMD) can account locally for over 80% of cassava root yield losses. [1]

[1] (Nutrient deficiencies are key constraints to grain legume productivity, p.2) The Double-Pot Method The double pot method is a rapid procedure used in diagnosing deficient plant nutrients in soils (Janssen, 1990). The set-up of the pots is as presented in Figure 1. Seedlings of test plants are sown in restricted quantity of soil placed in the upper pot (Pot 1), which has a gauze at the bottom. The growing roots pass through the gauze and reach the nutrient solution (in Pot 2) in which the desired test nutrient is omitted. The soil in Pot 1 is kept moist by irrigating with distilled water through a pipe filled with quartz. In this set up, two sources of nutrients are provided, which the plant can access simultaneously. The first is the test-soil itself, and the second the defined nutrient solution. By omitting one selected nutrient in the solution, the plant is forced to draw this nutrient from the soil. If the soil does not supply sufficient of this omitted nutrient, the plant will suffer from deficiency symptoms, such as limited growth and leaf deficiency symptoms. Such symptoms are visible in early growth stages, so that conclusions about further development and yield can be inferred after a few weeks.

Aﬂatoxins can negatively affect health of livestock and poultry due to contaminated feeds. Additionally, they signiﬁcantly limit the development of international trade as a result of strict regulation in high-value markets. Due to their high stability, aﬂatoxins are not only a problem during cropping, but also during storage, transport, processing, and handling steps. Consequently, innovative evidence-based technologies are urgently required to minimize aﬂatoxin exposure. Thus far, biological control has been developed as the most innovative potential technology of controlling aﬂatoxin contamination in crops, which uses competitive exclusion of toxigenic strains by non-toxigenic ones. This technology is commercially applied in groundnuts maize, cottonseed, and pistachios during pre-harvest stages. Some other effective technologies such as irradiation, ozone fumigation, chemical and biological control agents, and improved packaging materials can also minimize post-harvest aﬂatoxins contamination in agricultural products. However, integrated adoption of these pre- and post-harvest technologies is still required for sustainable solutions to reduce aﬂatoxins contamination, which enhances food security, alleviates malnutrition, and strengthens economic sustainability. © 2017 The Authors. [1] (Fertilizer and soil health for sustained crop production in sub-Sahara, p.6) Integrated soil fertility management The co-application of mineral fertilizers with organic inputs is a foundational principle of ISFM7 because neither input alone can sustainably support crop productivity and soil health in smallholder systems of SSA. Organic inputs such as crop residues, manure, and compost increase SOC, contribute to improved soil structure, water retention, cation exchange capacity, and biological activity, and help buffer soils against acidity and nutrient losses. However, when applied at quantities typically available on smallholder farms, they rarely release sufﬁcient nutrients to meet crop demand11. Mineral fertilizers, in contrast, provide concentrated and immediately available nutrients that enable rapid yield increases but are most effective when soil physical and biological constraints are alleviated through organic matter management. Evidence from ISFM research shows that positive interactions between mineral and organic nutrient sources frequently enhance agronomic use efﬁciency by improving nutrient capture and conversion efﬁciency, particularly on degraded or poorly responsive soils54. Fertilizer application can also stimulate biomass production, thereby increasing the availability of crop residues that could have a positive impact on SOC and protect soils against erosion, if produced and retained in sufﬁcient quantity. On the other hand, sustained application of organic inputs can rehabilitate degraded soils and restore their responsiveness to mineral fertilizers. These complementary effects demonstrate that integrated management of mineral fertilizers and organic resources is essential not only for maximizing shortterm yield responses but also for rebuilding soil fertility and ensuring longterm sustainability of cropping systems in SSA.

[3] (Sustainable insect pest management options for rice production in Sub-, p.12) 3.3. Nature-Based Control Options Nature-based control options, such as biological control, biopesticides, and semiochemicals, are characterized by their low impact on non-target organisms, as well as on human, animal, and environmental health. Biological control is an environmentally sustainable approach that uses natural predators, parasitoids, and beneficial microorganisms to regulate pest populations [262,263]. This method leverages the natural relationships between organisms to reduce pest numbers without relying on chemical pesticides. In SSA, several successful field-level applications demonstrate effectiveness in managing insect pests in rice production. In Nigeria, the introduction of Trichogramma wasps, which parasitize rice stem borer eggs, significantly reduced pest populations [38]. In addition, the use of the predatory beetles in the family Coccinellides has proven effective in managing the rice yellow mottle virus, by reducing populations of the aphids vectors, leading to increased yields [264]. In Tanzania, the use of predatory beetles in the family Coccinellidae has helped control rice leafhoppers [265]. In addition, the use of entomopathogenic fungi to control the rice weevil has shown promising results, with a 40% pest mortality [5,266]. In Tanzania, the adoption of IPM strategies, including the use of neem-based biopesticides, has reduced the reliance on synthetic pesticides and improved the sustainability of rice farming [267]. Additionally, in Zambia, the implementation of farmer field schools has empowered local farmers with knowledge and skills to manage pests using environmentally friendly methods. In Uganda and Tanzania, the introduction of pheromone traps has been effective in managing rice stem borer populations, reducing the need for synthetic pesticides and increasing rice [21]. In Uganda, the application of beneficial fungi such as Beauveria bassiana has proven successful in managing rice hispa infestations [268]. In West Africa, the release of parasitoid wasps like Anagrus spp. helped to limit the prevalence of rice gall midge [269]. In Benin and Côte d’Ivoire, the fungus Neozygites tanajoa has effectively managed the cassava green mite, demonstrating its potential for broader pest management applications [270]. In Kenya, the introduction of parasitoid wasps to control the rice yellow stem borer resulted in a 50% reduction in pest populations and a corresponding increase in rice yields [38,271]. By reducing pest populations through natural regulation, these agents help maintain biodiversity, improve crop resilience, and minimize harm to non-target organisms. Continued investment in research, farmer training, and regional adaptation of biocontrol technologies is essential for scaling up their adoption. [1] (Guide to Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Surveillance, control, and product, p.15) Most banana varieties produce several offshoots (known as suckers) from the same underground corm, each of which can grow into a new pseudostem bearing a bunch of bananas. Once the pseudostem of the mother plant has flowered and the fruit is harvested, that pseudostem dies back. Meanwhile, one of the suckers (known as the maiden sucker) takes over, grows, flowers, and fruits in the following cycle. Because new shoots continuously replace the old, the banana plant as a whole persists year after year, making it a perennial. However, each individual pseudostem follows a cycle more like an annual: grow flower fruit die. During the rainy season, a sucker produces an average of two leaves per month, while in the dry season, growth slows significantly, to perhaps just one leaf every five weeks. New leaves are generally larger than the older ones when adequate soil fertility and moisture are available. An excess of suckers on a mother plant can lead to reduced bunch weight. Therefore, farmers often manage the number of suckers that develop by pruning (desuckering).

The lifespan of stored seeds largely depends on the environmental conditions within the store, particularly temperature and humidity. In the case of the banana aphid and BBTV, a viruliferous banana aphid carries the BBTV and can transmit it to a banana plant when it feeds on the plant sap. Virus indexing. In the context of plant viruses, virus indexing is the process of testing plants for the presence of specific viruses to ensure they are free from infection. Virus indexing is particularly important in agriculture and horticulture, where virus-free plants are essential for maintaining healthy crops and preventing the spread of diseases. Common methods of virus indexing include: • Serological tests, such as ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay), which detect viral proteins. Molecular tests, such as PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction), which detect viral genetic material. Virus transmission. In the context of BBTD, virus transmission refers to the movement of BBTV from an infected banana plant to a healthy one. This occurs primarily through banana aphids (Pentalonia nigronervosa), which acquire the virus by feeding on the sap of an infected plant and then spread it by feeding on healthy plants. BBTV can also spread through infected planting materials, such as suckers taken from an infected mother plant. Water sucker. A water sucker of banana is a weak vegetative shoot with broad leaves and poor attachment to the mother corm, which generally develops into an unproductive banana plant. Water suckers are not recommended for fruit production.

[2] (Soil fertility management in Babati: A practical guide on good agricul, p.11) Land preparation Prepare your land on time to ensure other field operations, such as planting, are not delayed. Being timely enhances utilization of soil moisture. If the field has to be tilled, it’s important to consider the direction of the slope. Ploughing across the contour (up and down) should be avoided to minimize soil erosion. Such ploughing allows transfers and loss of essential plant nutrients and deposits them on fields located down the slope i.e., flat fields and sometimes to dams, lakes and the ocean. Ploughing across the slope (i.e., along the contours) increases water infiltration into the soil and reduces soil erosion down the slope. If the width of your field is narrow and ploughing along the contour is not practical for tractors, try other methods including adopting conservation agricultural practices (CA) or use hand hoe instead of tractor to plough. It is important to avoid land degradation because it requires great effort and time to correct. In a season, agricultural fields experiencing soil degradation produce on average 4 bags per acre less than non-degraded maize fields. The amount of yield lost depends on level of degradation.

In some East African countries, banana provides up to 60% of the daily calorie intake. Uganda has the highest consumption at >0.5 kg person−1 day−1 . There has been a global decline in banana production for the past 40 years [1] with the current yield being a fraction of its potential [3,4]. The banana weevil (Cosmopolites sordidus) and a multifaceted array of plant-parasitic nematodes (PPNs) are among the critical biotic constraints to banana production [5]. Radopholus similis is generally viewed as the most damaging nematode pest of bananas [6–8], but in East Africa a complex of species, comprising R. similis, Helicotylenchus multicinctus, Pratylenchus spp. and Meloidogyne spp. create a combined community that affects bananas [9–11]. The community composition varies by locality, climate and banana genotype [10]. Most of the developmental stages of the weevil (eggs, larvae and pupa) are found in the corms of infested plants, while the adults are found in crop residues, sheltering in or around the corms, and between the leaf sheaths in close association with the banana corms. In contrast, all development stages of the nematodes reside in the corm and roots of infested plants [12]. Despite the free movement of adult weevils and their ability to infest new fields, the dissemination of both weevils and nematodes is primarily through contaminated planting materials. Most banana farms in the region are plagued with both weevils and PPNs, usually in combination. Heavy infestation of banana fields by both pests can result in up to 100% yield losses [13]. The physical damage caused by weevils and nematodes is also a crucial entry point for banana pathogens, while weevils are also known to act as a vector for some banana diseases [14,15]. A key strategy to improve banana production therefore relies on developing appropriate and effective management options against both the weevil and the PPNs. The use of fungal endophytes in the management of both the weevil and nematodes has previously been shown to be effective. The non-pathogenic Fusarium oxysporum isolate V5w2 effectively colonized banana plants without penalty to the host, and even improved plant growth [16–18]. Similarly, the entomopathogen Beauveria bassiana isolate WA effectively colonized banana plants without hampering plant vigor or development [19]. Endophytic colonization of F. oxysporum also led to reduced nematode damage and infection levels [17,20–22], while colonization by B. bassiana reduced weevil density and damage [23,24]. The majority of studies, however, have been undertaken in pots in the screenhouse, although some limited field work has been conducted [25]. Field studies in Uganda demonstrated that following inoculation with F. oxysporum, colonization persisted for up to 6 months [26], and that bunch weight and yield during the first crop cycle was higher when enhanced with F. oxysporum compared with uninoculated controls [25]. There is limited information about the dual inoculation of F. oxysporum and B. bassiana in banana and the potential effect on plant pest and disease resistance and effect on yield. The current study was consequently designed to assess the performance of single and combined inoculation of F. oxysporum and B. bassiana into tissue-cultured banana plants to determine endophyte colonization persistence, effect on weevil damage and PPN infection levels, plant growth and yield under field conditions, simulating smallholder farming conditions in Uganda. 2. Mycotoxins can be cytotoxic, genotoxic, mutagenic, and teratogenic, and they are persistent threats to human and animal health. This perspective assesses opportunities to prevent mycotoxigenic fungal infection in maize seeds produced for sowing as an important starting point of crop contamination. Being timely enhances utilization of soil moisture. If the field has to be tilled, it’s important to consider the direction of the slope. Naturally infected faba bean plants showed shoot proliferation, witches’ broom, stunting, phyllody, and yellowing and little leaves [165–167]. In Yemen, phytoplasma disease of faba bean, caused by Mycoplasma-like organisms (MLO), was recorded in Wadi Hadhramaut in the spring of 1990 [168]. The symptoms of infected chickpea include pale green leaves with smaller leaﬂets and bushy appearance due to axillary shoot proliferation, abnormal green structures develop in place of normal ﬂowers, and the pod set is aﬀected [169]. Phytoplasma can be managed by controlling leafhopper vectors and removing infected plants, but neither prevention method has been fully eﬀective in ﬁeld conditions. [3] (Mycotoxin concentrations in rice are affected by chalkiness, grain sha, p.1) Abstract Mycotoxins such as aflatoxins (AFs), fumonisins (FBs), zearalenone (ZEN), and deoxynivalenol (DON) pose a risk to public health due to their carcinogenic potency (AFs and FBs) and anti-nutritional effects. The hazards associated with mycotoxins are accentuated where food management practices, control, and regulatory systems from farm to plate are sub-optimal. Information on the frequency of these mycotoxins in rice commercialized in markets in sub-Sahara Africa (SSA) is limited. The current study examined AF concentrations in 527 rice samples collected from 54 markets in five SSA countries. Grain quality characteristics, processing methods, and origin of samples were contrasted with toxin levels. In total, 72% of the samples had detectable AFs levels (range = 3.0 to 89.8 µg/kg). Multivariate analysis revealed that length-to-width ratio (p < 0.0001), mixed variety for width (p = 0.04), and chalkiness (p = 0.009) significantly influenced aflatoxin concentrations. Slender grains had higher AFs concentrations than bold and medium grains (p < 0.0001). Possible strategies to mitigate mycotoxin contamination in rice include improving grain quality traits and practicing proper drying and hermetic storage before and after milling. These findings provide valuable insights for both domestic and international actors in establishing and strengthening regulations and management systems to mitigate rice mycotoxin contamination. Terraces can be dug and soil placed on the upper Fanya juu or lower Fanya chini side of the slope. ▶ Fanya juu terraces enhance water infiltration and deposition of eroded soil in the portion of land adjacent to the terrace (Figure 10). Up to 70% of runoff water infiltrates into the terrace, thus preventing waterlogging of bean fields. ▶ If the amount of runoff is higher than can be controlled through a Fanya juu terrace, placing soil on the lower side of the terrace (Fanya chini) allows collection and conservation of runoff water inside the terrace. ▶ The soil bund on the upper or lower side of the terrace can be stabilized by planting grass strips and forage crops such as Napier grass or agroforestry trees. Other water conservation structures include retention ditches and infiltration pits that collect and retain runoff water until it slowly seeps into the soil. The two structures are ideal for bean fields in dry areas where wet seasons are followed by prolonged dry spells. [3] (Production and economic performance of women-led grass seed and hay en, p.7) 4.2 Production and restoration model The production sequence allows the groups to obtain two products from the same grass stand. Seed is collected first as the primary product. After seed harvesting, the remaining grass is cut and baled as hay. This sequencing improves resource use because the group earns income from both the reproductive and vegetative components of the crop rather than treating the post-seed biomass as waste. However, participants noted an important trade-off: by the time the seed matures, the grass is relatively old and fibrous, resulting in hay with lower protein content, digestibility and overall feeding value. The hay may therefore be more suitable as dry-season basal feed and may require supplementation with higher-quality feeds, particularly for productive livestock. The first harvest was reported to have performed below expectations because rainfall was below average. In the following year, water bunds were introduced within the production site. Participants reported a marked improvement in grass growth and yield after bund construction. The experience suggests that the moisture-conservation function of the bunds is central to the reliability of the enterprise, especially where rainfall is erratic. Water bunds are also constructed across the surrounding rangelands. Participants associate these restored areas with increased forage availability for livestock and wildlife, extending the benefits beyond the immediate enterprise plots. Access is temporarily restricted to allow the vegetation to establish and mature, after which the areas are opened for grazing. Unlike the enterprise plots, these restored rangelands are used exclusively for community grazing.

Conventional ox-ploughing and shallow tillage often fail to break hardpan layers. This limits root penetration and reduces the amount of rainfall that can infiltrate and remain available to crops. Generally, soil in the Tanganika region is good for bean production. Distribution of acidic soil in eastern DRC is as illustrated in Figure 2. It is advisable to conduct soil analysis to determine the acidity before planting. If soil analysis services are inaccessible, check for nutrient deficiency symptoms in your crop as described in Section 1.3.2 of this manual. You can also check weeds such as fern, cogon grass, and spreading dayflowers because they thrive in acidic soils. Beans grown in acidic soil have low response to applied fertilizer. In eastern DRC, acidic soil produces less than 400 kg/ha (<160 kg/acre) of beans. Under good agronomic practices, lime application can increase bush bean yield from 400 kg/ha (160 kg/acre) to more than 1,000 kg/ha (450 kg/acre). Lime products are available in granular or powder form: ▶ Calcium oxide (calcitic lime): CaO ▶ Calcium carbonate (calcitic lime): CaCO3 ▶ Dolomite (dolomitic lime): CaMg(CO3)2 The recommended lime application rate is 200 to 500 kg/acre, but the rate could vary depending on the soil acidity level. Applying lower rates of lime at frequent seasonal intervals is also effective for helping to overcome soil acidity. Broadcasting and incorporating lime in the soil can control soil acidity for several years. To moderate soil fertility for a longer period, liming can be accompanied by other ISFM practices such as manure application and crop residue retention. If lime is not accessible, apply well-composted manure more frequently to amend soil acidity. Other cultural methods of overcoming soil acidity challenges include application of organic matter in the soil in the form of crop residues, mulch, or manure.

FAW management options in the newly invaded areas are limited and mainly rely on the use of synthetic pesticides. Since there is a risk of resistance development against pesticides in addition to the negative environmental and human health impacts, other effective, sustainable, and cost-efficient control alternatives are desired. [3] (A guide to standardized methods of analysis for soil, water, plant, an, p.36) Carbonates Various primary and secondary carbonates are found in soils. The most common types are calcite (CaCO3) and dolomite [CaMg(CO3)2]. Less common soil carbonates are sodium carbonate (Na2CO3) and siderite (FeCO3). Carbonates buffer soil pH and are an indication of the relative abundance of bases. Besides pedogenic implications, carbonate minerals play an important role in soil management (Doner and Lynn, 1989). The distribution and amount of carbonates influence soil fertility, erodibility, and available water capacity. Calcimetric and titration methods have been used as standard methods for estimation of carbonates in soils. Both methods are equally applicable for determining carbonates in the soil. However, the calcimetric method is rapid and does not need more chemicals, whereas the titration method is slow and labor intensive. Gypsum Gypsum is present in soils in the form of calcium sulphate dihydrate (CaSO4.2H2O). The presence of gypsum and calcium carbonates interferes with some laboratory measurements including cation exchange capacity and particle-size distribution. This impedes interpretation of soil analytical data for land evaluation and mapping, land utilization, reclamation, and recommendation of fertilizer. The laboratory methods used for the analysis of gypsiferous soils are the same as those used for non-gypsiferous soils. Acetone precipitation of gypsum, which involves redissolving of the gypsum precipitate using distilled water and measurement of the electrical conductivity, is a common method for estimation of gypsum in soils (Sayegh et al., 1978).

[2] (Guide to Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Surveillance, control, and product, p.15) Most banana varieties produce several offshoots (known as suckers) from the same underground corm, each of which can grow into a new pseudostem bearing a bunch of bananas. Once the pseudostem of the mother plant has flowered and the fruit is harvested, that pseudostem dies back. Meanwhile, one of the suckers (known as the maiden sucker) takes over, grows, flowers, and fruits in the following cycle. Because new shoots continuously replace the old, the banana plant as a whole persists year after year, making it a perennial. However, each individual pseudostem follows a cycle more like an annual: grow flower fruit die. During the rainy season, a sucker produces an average of two leaves per month, while in the dry season, growth slows significantly, to perhaps just one leaf every five weeks. New leaves are generally larger than the older ones when adequate soil fertility and moisture are available. An excess of suckers on a mother plant can lead to reduced bunch weight. Therefore, farmers often manage the number of suckers that develop by pruning (desuckering).

[1] (Sustainable insect pest management options for rice production in Sub-, p.1) Major insect pests such as stem borers, leafhoppers, and rice bugs are increasingly threatening rice production in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). Sustainable pest management is vital to protect yields and promote agricultural sustainability. Integrated Pest Management (IPM) offers a balanced approach, combining multiple pest management strategies to reduce reliance on chemical inputs and safeguard ecosystems. Key strategies include weed and alternative host plant control, which limits pest habitats, and the use of resistant or tolerant rice varieties that naturally deter insect damage. Biopesticides—derived from natural organisms—are emerging as eco-friendly alternatives to synthetic chemicals. While chemical control remains common, its overuse can harm beneficial insects and the environment. Biological control, using predators and parasitoids, supports long-term pest suppression. A comparison between cultural, chemical, and biological methods demonstrates the value of context-specific solutions tailored to local farming systems. Advances in biotechnology, such as genetic resistance and molecular diagnostics, offer promising tools for future pest management. However, challenges persist, including limited farmer awareness, infrastructure gaps, and climate variability. Future directions should focus on farmer education, policy support, and adaptive research to strengthen sustainable pest management in SSA and ensure resilient rice production systems.

Crop Rotation This method disrupts the life cycles of pests that are specific to certain crops, reducing their populations over time. Evidence of its efficacy was demonstrated in rice, where crop rotation had improved soil health, crop yield, and pest control, using big data [105]. In the context of rice production across Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), several countries have demonstrated the value of this practice in pest control. In Nigeria, rotating rice with cowpeas significantly reduced the population of rice stem borers [106]. In Tanzania, alternating rice with maize effectively managed rice leafhoppers) [107]. In Uganda, rotating rice with groundnuts helped to control the incidence of rice yellow mottle virus, often spread by insect vectors [107]. In Kenya, rotating rice with soybeans reduced the incidence of rice gall midge [108]. In Ghana, rotating rice with cassava proved successful in managing rice hispa infestations [108]. Beyond pest suppression, crop rotation contributes to soil fertility maintenance and the mitigation of soil-borne diseases [109]. These examples demonstrate how crop rotation is not only a key pest management strategy but also improves the overall agroecosystem resilience.

The probability of stress represents the fraction of growing-season days during which simulated root-zone soil moisture is insufficient to meet crop evapotranspiration demand, with higher values indicating more frequent occurrences of soil moisture stress during the growing season. Conversely, regions with low SI values (< 0.6), notably in the eastern and southeastern lowlands, align with high probabilities of stress (≥ 0.6), reflecting persistent soil moisture deficits throughout the growing period. Intermediate SI values (0.6–0.8) are associated with moderate stress probabilities, highlighting zones where crops experience intermittent but recurrent moisture constraints. Crop-specific differences further reinforce this relationship, and legumes such as common bean, cowpea, mung bean, and grass pea tend to maintain higher SI and lower stress probabilities over larger areas, whereas chickpea, faba bean, field pea, lentil, and soybean display lower SI and higher stress probabilities, particularly in moisture-limited environments. Together, SI and probability of stress provide complementary metrics that capture both the adequacy and reliability of soil moisture supply, offering a robust framework for evaluating the suitability and risk of post-rainfall legume production under varying climatic and soil conditions.

[3] (Potential of residual soil moisture for supporting post-season legume , p.20) The integrated assessment of crop water requirements, soil moisture availability, seasonal soil water satisfaction (SI), probability of stress, and stage-specific water deficits underscores the importance of aligning crop choice, planting strategies, and water management with local hydroclimatic conditions. Post-rainfall legume cultivation is most viable in regions with high SI and low stress probabilities, particularly in the central, southern, and southwestern highlands, where residual soil moisture can reliably support crop water demand throughout the growing season. In contrast, eastern and southeastern lowlands exhibit persistently low SI, high probabilities of stress, and pronounced mid-season water deficits, necessitating more cautious crop selection and management. In these moisture-limited environments, drought-tolerant and short-duration legumes, combined with moistureconservation practices such as early planting, mulching, reduced tillage, and improved soil fertility management, are essential to enhance water-use efficiency. Across all regions, the mid-season growth stage emerges as the most water-sensitive phase, highlighting the need to synchronize sowing dates with residual soil moisture availability and, where feasible, explore supplemental irrigation options. Future research will further account for climatic heterogeneity by classifying rainfed agricultural areas into distinct rainfall regimes using data-driven clustering approaches. This regime-based framework will enable improved understanding and prediction of residual soil moisture dynamics under varying rainfall distributions and will support the development of climateinformed recommendations for crop selection, sowing windows, and sustainable, climate-resilient rainfed agricultural planning.

[1] (Effective altruism as an ethical lens on research priorities, p.1) ABSTRACT Effective altruism is an ethical framework for identifying the greatest potential benefits from investments. Here, we apply effective altruism concepts to maximize research benefits through identification of priority stakeholders, pathosystems, and research questions and technologies. Priority stakeholders for research benefits may include smallholder farmers who have not yet attained the minimal standards set out by the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals; these farmers would often have the most to gain from better crop disease management, if their management problems are tractable. In wildlands, prioritization has been based on the risk of extirpating keystone species, protecting ecosystem services, and preserving wild resources of importance to vulnerable people. Pathosystems may be prioritized based on yield and quality loss, and also factors such as whether other researchers would be unlikely to replace the research efforts if efforts were withdrawn, such as in the case of orphan crops and orphan pathosystems. Research products that help build sustainable and resilient systems can be particularly beneficial. The “value of information” from research can be evaluated in epidemic networks and landscapes, to identify priority locations for both benefits to individuals and to constrain regional epidemics. As decision-making becomes more consolidated and more networked in digital agricultural systems, the range of ethical considerations expands. Low-likelihood but high-damage scenarios such as generalist doomsday pathogens may be research priorities because of the extreme potential cost. Regional microbiomes constitute a commons, and avoiding the “tragedy of the microbiome commons” may depend on shifting research products from “common pool goods” to “public goods” or other categories. We provide suggestions for how individual researchers and funders may make altruism-driven research more effective. Keywords: analytical and theoretical plant pathology, disease control and pest management, ecology and epidemiology, genetics and resistance

The lack of soil cover also means that weed management through soil mulch is unachievable. Cultivating beans and other crops on the same piece of land facilitates the exploitation of nutrients from different soil layers at different times, thus preventing nutrient mining. [3] (How maize seed systems can contribute to the control of mycotoxigenic , p.1) Abstract: Mycotoxins are toxic secondary metabolites produced by fungi on agricultural produce. Mycotoxins can be cytotoxic, genotoxic, mutagenic, and teratogenic, and they are persistent threats to human and animal health. Consumption of mycotoxin-contaminated maize can cause cancer and even sudden death. Health hazards can also occur from consuming products from animals fed with mycotoxin-contaminated feed or forage. The main mode of spread of mycotoxigenic fungi is through air-borne spores originating from soil or plant debris, although some fungi can also spread through infected seed-to-seedling transmission, ultimately followed by contamination of the harvestable product. This perspective assesses opportunities to prevent mycotoxigenic fungal infection in maize seeds produced for sowing as an important starting point of crop contamination. A case study of Nigeria showed infection in all tested farmer-produced, seed company, and foundation seed samples. A schematic overview of the formal and informal seed systems is presented to analyze their contribution to fungal infection and mycotoxin contamination in the maize value chain, as well as to set criteria for successful control. We recommend an integrated approach to control mycotoxigenic fungal infection, including resistant varieties and other control methods during seed production, grain production, and grain storage, with an important role in maintaining seed health. Early and accurate detection of BBTD is essential for effective management and control, as it enables timely interventions that can prevent further spread. Unfortunately, many farmers are unfamiliar with the symptoms of BBTD, especially when the disease first appears in new areas, making early detection and control more difficult. Plants that are infected by aphid transmission of BBTV In plants that are infected by aphid transmission of the virus, BBTD symptoms may appear at any stage, from young plants to mature ones. As the disease progresses, symptoms accumulate, with early signs persisting into intermediate and later stages. When a banana plant becomes infected with BBTV from a banana aphid, BBTD symptoms will usually appear between 3–4 weeks and 4 months after infection. The set-up of the pots is as presented in Figure 1. Seedlings of test plants are sown in restricted quantity of soil placed in the upper pot (Pot 1), which has a gauze at the bottom. The growing roots pass through the gauze and reach the nutrient solution (in Pot 2) in which the desired test nutrient is omitted. The soil in Pot 1 is kept moist by irrigating with distilled water through a pipe filled with quartz. In this set up, two sources of nutrients are provided, which the plant can access simultaneously. The first is the test-soil itself, and the second the defined nutrient solution. By omitting one selected nutrient in the solution, the plant is forced to draw this nutrient from the soil. If the soil does not supply sufficient of this omitted nutrient, the plant will suffer from deficiency symptoms, such as limited growth and leaf deficiency symptoms. What appears as the trunk of a banana plant is not a true stem like those of woody plants but is actually a pseudostem formed by tightly packed layers of overlapping leaf sheaths (Fig. 5). Depending on the banana variety, the pseudostem rises to a height of 1.5 to 5 meters. The large underground corm (also known as the rhizome) is the true stem of the banana plant. The corm functions as a storage organ, storing nutrients and energy for the plant, and serves as the base from which the plant’s roots, pseudostem, and secondary shoots (suckers) emerge. • The corm and roots anchor the banana plant to the ground. The roots, growing mainly on the sides of the corm, grow to a depth of about 20 cm and spread approximately 2 meters radially from the corm. The banana plant produces offshoots, called suckers, from the corm. These suckers develop into new plants, forming a mat (a cluster) of interconnected plants. These plants, connected through the corm, can be compared to branches of a tree joined to a single stem.

[3] (Guide to Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Surveillance, control, and product, p.15) Most banana varieties produce several offshoots (known as suckers) from the same underground corm, each of which can grow into a new pseudostem bearing a bunch of bananas. Once the pseudostem of the mother plant has flowered and the fruit is harvested, that pseudostem dies back. Meanwhile, one of the suckers (known as the maiden sucker) takes over, grows, flowers, and fruits in the following cycle. Because new shoots continuously replace the old, the banana plant as a whole persists year after year, making it a perennial. However, each individual pseudostem follows a cycle more like an annual: grow flower fruit die. During the rainy season, a sucker produces an average of two leaves per month, while in the dry season, growth slows significantly, to perhaps just one leaf every five weeks. New leaves are generally larger than the older ones when adequate soil fertility and moisture are available. An excess of suckers on a mother plant can lead to reduced bunch weight. Therefore, farmers often manage the number of suckers that develop by pruning (desuckering).

Seed longevity is an important agronomic factor, which, if not maximized, can lead to loss in seed vigor and viability during storage, thus negatively impacting seedling establishment and the overall yield. It is important for genebanks to predict the longevity of their accessions as an unexpected loss in viability will incur more frequent regeneration, which is costly economically and risky genetically.4,26,27 This is particularly problematic for species that are inherently short-lived as they already have short regeneration intervals. In comparison with cowpea (oil content of 1%),28 which has a predicted longevity (r) of 301 years under medium-term storage (6.1% MC and 5C) at IITA (estimated using the SID),23 soya bean (oil content of 21%29) seeds are relatively short-lived with an estimated longevity of only 92 years based on the viability constants given in Ellis et al.30 and Dickie et al.31. As in cultivated rice, longevity in legumes increases during seed development, particularly during seed maturation.32,33 Previous research on rice has provided evidence that seed quality15 and subsequent seed longevity12–14,16 can be improved ex planta by drying seeds immediately after harvest, which are still within the maturation drying phase of seed development (MCs close to 16.5%),12–14 for an initial period at a high temperature (45C–60C) before final drying at a lower temperature and humidity, as recommended in the Genebank Standards.2 The results of this study have major implications for genebanks globally as it has shown that such benefits are not limited to rice, and potentially, a two-stage drying procedure could also improve storage longevity of other orthodox species. Post-rainfall legume cultivation is most viable in regions with high SI and low stress probabilities, particularly in the central, southern, and southwestern highlands, where residual soil moisture can reliably support crop water demand throughout the growing season. In contrast, eastern and southeastern lowlands exhibit persistently low SI, high probabilities of stress, and pronounced mid-season water deficits, necessitating more cautious crop selection and management. In these moisture-limited environments, drought-tolerant and short-duration legumes, combined with moistureconservation practices such as early planting, mulching, reduced tillage, and improved soil fertility management, are essential to enhance water-use efficiency. Future research will further account for climatic heterogeneity by classifying rainfed agricultural areas into distinct rainfall regimes using data-driven clustering approaches. The probability of stress represents the fraction of growing-season days during which simulated root-zone soil moisture is insufficient to meet crop evapotranspiration demand, with higher values indicating more frequent occurrences of soil moisture stress during the growing season. Conversely, regions with low SI values (< 0.6), notably in the eastern and southeastern lowlands, align with high probabilities of stress (≥ 0.6), reflecting persistent soil moisture deficits throughout the growing period. Intermediate SI values (0.6–0.8) are associated with moderate stress probabilities, highlighting zones where crops experience intermittent but recurrent moisture constraints. Crop-specific differences further reinforce this relationship, and legumes such as common bean, cowpea, mung bean, and grass pea tend to maintain higher SI and lower stress probabilities over larger areas, whereas chickpea, faba bean, field pea, lentil, and soybean display lower SI and higher stress probabilities, particularly in moisture-limited environments. Understanding these fundamentals is crucial for farmers and agricultural practitioners, particularly when addressing challenges such as Banana Bunchy Top Disease (BBTD). The chapter also introduces key terms that are used when describing BBTD symptoms and aspects of its management and control. Wild bananas are primarily diploid species, notably Musa acuminata (AA genome) and Musa balbisiana (BB genome). Domesticated bananas are mostly sterile triploid hybrids with combinations of the A and B genomes (e.g., AAA, AAB, ABB).6 Musa acuminata and Musa balbisiana reproduce sexually and produce seeded fruit, whereas domesticated bananas reproduce vegetatively and are typically seedless (Fig. 3). Bananas and plantains (genus Musa) originated in Southeast Asia, which still holds the greatest diversity of wild and cultivated species. Cultivating beans and other crops on the same piece of land facilitates the exploitation of nutrients from different soil layers at different times, thus preventing nutrient mining. Living organisms are also able to derive food from diverse plant sources. Crop diversity provides food and habitat for insects and could decrease pest attacks on beans while simultaneously enhancing pollination. You can maximize biodiversity through the following methods: ▶ Crop rotation: Cereal crops such as sorghum and maize or tubers such as cassava and potatoes are planted in one season and rotated with beans in subsequent seasons. ▶ Intercropping: A row of a cereal or tuber crop is alternated with beans on the same land and in the same season. ▶ Agroforestry: raising crops such as beans and trees on the same farm. Roots of trees grow deep into the soil and pump nutrients back to the soil surface. Above the ground, the trees protect beans against strong winds and direct raindrops. ▶ Cover crops help to increase soil protection, moisture retention, nutrient supply, and weed suppression. ▶ Forage strips, especially leguminous forages (Desmodium, Sesbania, etc.), reinforce soils (especially on sloping fields), fix nitrogen, and are also fed to livestock. ▶ Application of organic-rich nutrient resources such as manure and compost, and bean residues after harvest. ▶ Minimizing off-season grazing ensures livestock does not destroy vegetation, thus enhancing plant diversity. ▶ Maintaining a rich root network from diverse species of plants (Figure 2).

Grains may be lost in the pre-harvest, harvest, and post-harvest stages. Pre-harvest losses occur before the process of harvesting begins, and may be due to insects, weeds, and diseases. Soil samples (n = 3387) were collected across the area using multistage and random sampling techniques, and samples were analyzed for pH, soil organic carbon (SOC), macronutrients (N, P, K, S, Ca and Mg), micronutrients (S, B, Zn, Mn and Fe) content, and effective cation exchange capacity (ECEC). Introduction Banana (Musa spp.) is an important food and income crop across a wide range of agroecological zones and cropping systems in the African Great Lakes region (AGLR) [1]. This region produces about one third of the world’s banana production [1]. The crop provides 30–60% of food energy requirements for over 70 million people [2,3] in this region that comprises of Burundi, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo), Rwanda, Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda. The AGLR is characterized by a high population density, with the highest population densities of 435 and 499 inhabitants per km2 , respectively reported in Burundi and Rwanda [4]. About 70–90% of the population in this region is employed in agriculture as smallholder farmers [5–8]. This high population density and heavy dependence on agriculture has resulted in small and fragmented farms characterized by declining soil fertility. For example, farm landholdings in banana producing areas of Rwanda, Burundi, and eastern DR Congo have been reported to vary between 0.5 and 2 ha [5]. To compound the problem of small and fragmented farm sizes, and declining soil fertility, external inputs such as manure and inorganic fertilizers are not widely used in the region [9]. For example, in Uganda in 2013, only 2.8% of the land under key crops received fertilizers (accounting for 30 kg ha−1 of fertilizer on the fertilized soils), with banana accounting for 25% of this land area [10]. Moreover, previously important cultural practices for managing soil fertility, and pests and diseases, such as crop rotation, agroforestry, shifting cultivation, and fallowing, are no longer feasible or optimally practiced due to the small farm sizes and more intensive farming systems [11,12]. van Asten et al. [13] report soil infertility as one of the major constraints to banana production in the region. Searching for sustainable nutrient management options that do not compromise other production objectives is thus critical. Farmers commonly intercrop banana with other annual crops, including legumes in a bid to optimally use the available land and mitigate possible risks [12,14,15]. The incorporation of food and/or fodder legumes within banana fields has been reported to increase land and resource use efficiency of smallholder banana farms; suppress weeds; and minimize risks related to climate change and pests and diseases [15–18]. Similar observations have been reported for legume intercrops with other crops such as maize, cassava, and agroforestry trees [19–22]. Intercropping with legumes may also be a strategy to offset soil fertility depletion [17,23]. McIntyre et al. [24] observed some legume intercrops (Canavalia ensiformis, Mucuna pruriens and Tephrosia vogelii) to exacerbate banana nematode root and corm damage, while weevil larvae-linked corm damage did not significantly change. McIntyre et al. [24], however, observed no significant yield effects on banana and an increase in land use efficiency. In a recent study, [18] observed a decline in the severity of bean foliar diseases, Septoria brown spots, and angular leaf spot under banana shade. A high functional biodiversity and interaction between crop species has also been reported to enhance agroecosystem sustainability [25]. However, the integration of annual crops in banana fields across several landscapes in the AGLR has been hampered by the shading effect from the banana leaf canopy. As a coping strategy, farmers often prune banana leaves to allow for light penetration to the shorter understory crops [18,26]. Leaf pruning has been reported to reduce the productivity of the banana crop [26,27] and overall economic efficiency of the intercrop [18]. This practice additionally enhances the risk for spreading Xanthomonas wilt (XW) of banana, a key constraint to banana production in the AGLR [28]. Given the negative effects of leaf pruning and the associated risk of spreading XW disease, leaf pruning could undermine the benefits associated with a high level of functional biodiversity.

[2] (Guide to Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Surveillance, control, and product, p.18) This chapter introduces banana propagation methods, highlighting sucker propagation, macropropagation, and micropropagation by tissue culture. The importance of disease-free planting materials for improving production is emphasized, while discussing the limitations of each method for smallholder farmers. Cultivated banana plants are propagated vegetatively (asexually) because they are typically seedless. Vegetative propagation generates new plants that are genetically identical to the mother plant, maintaining the same desirable traits such as fruit quality. This is essential for ensuring the consistency and reliability of the crop. For further information on propagation using suckers, refer to section 7.1 Information Resources: The banana plant, propagation and best management practices. A major challenge in banana production is the limited availability of high-quality, virus-free planting materials. However, macropropagation and micropropagation, when combined with virus indexing (testing for BBTV and other viruses), are highly effective methods for producing large quantities of clean planting materials. Propagation by suckers is the principal method used by smallholder farmers because it is cheap and does not require sophisticated skills. The process involves carefully cutting a sucker along with a piece of the corm from the mother plant and then transplanting it.
[3] (Guide to Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Surveillance, control, and product, p.64) Viruliferous means carrying and capable of transmitting a virus. In the case of the banana aphid and BBTV, a viruliferous banana aphid carries the BBTV and can transmit it to a banana plant when it feeds on the plant sap. Virus indexing. In the context of plant viruses, virus indexing is the process of testing plants for the presence of specific viruses to ensure they are free from infection. Virus indexing is particularly important in agriculture and horticulture, where virus-free plants are essential for maintaining healthy crops and preventing the spread of diseases. Common methods of virus indexing include: • Serological tests, such as ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay), which detect viral proteins. Molecular tests, such as PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction), which detect viral genetic material. Virus transmission. In the context of BBTD, virus transmission refers to the movement of BBTV from an infected banana plant to a healthy one. This occurs primarily through banana aphids (Pentalonia nigronervosa), which acquire the virus by feeding on the sap of an infected plant and then spread it by feeding on healthy plants. BBTV can also spread through infected planting materials, such as suckers taken from an infected mother plant. Water sucker. A water sucker of banana is a weak vegetative shoot with broad leaves and poor attachment to the mother corm, which generally develops into an unproductive banana plant. Water suckers are not recommended for fruit production.

S. bradys is considered the most important species. Low levels of infection on seed tubers, which may go undetected, provide inoculum to the next crop, and lead to heavy losses of infected tubers during storage. RKNs have traditionally been less of a problem. Meloidogyne arenaria, Meloidogyne enterolobii, Meloidogyne incognita, and Meloidogyne javanica are the species associated with yield loss in yam. Although RKNs are also seedborne, significant infection occurs in the field. Spatial distribution of the Probability of Soil Moisture Stress for selected legume crops across Ethiopia. The probability of stress represents the fraction of growing-season days during which simulated root-zone soil moisture is insufficient to meet crop evapotranspiration demand, with higher values indicating more frequent occurrences of soil moisture stress during the growing season. Conversely, regions with low SI values (< 0.6), notably in the eastern and southeastern lowlands, align with high probabilities of stress (≥ 0.6), reflecting persistent soil moisture deficits throughout the growing period. Intermediate SI values (0.6–0.8) are associated with moderate stress probabilities, highlighting zones where crops experience intermittent but recurrent moisture constraints. Crop-specific differences further reinforce this relationship, and legumes such as common bean, cowpea, mung bean, and grass pea tend to maintain higher SI and lower stress probabilities over larger areas, whereas chickpea, faba bean, field pea, lentil, and soybean display lower SI and higher stress probabilities, particularly in moisture-limited environments. Together, SI and probability of stress provide complementary metrics that capture both the adequacy and reliability of soil moisture supply, offering a robust framework for evaluating the suitability and risk of post-rainfall legume production under varying climatic and soil conditions.

Over the years, geostatistics is one of the most eﬀective tools used to study the variation and spatial distribution of soil nutrients [8,17]. Geostatistics is a tool for estimating soil property values in nonsampled areas or areas with scanty sampling. It provides a set of statistical tools for the description of spatial patterns, quantitative modeling of spatial continuity, spatial prediction, and uncertainty assessment [18]. Scientists have also used this tool to develop spatial variability maps of soil properties [19–21]. Furthermore, information obtained from spatial variability maps have been used in delineating relatively homogeneous nutrient management zones (MZs) [8, 15, 22, 23]. Nutrient management zones are the most general approach used to manage ﬁeld spatial variability [24] because MZs are symmetric subregions with similar characteristics aﬀecting yield or with the same yield productivity [25, 26]. Nutrient management zones can help address economic and environmental concerns resulting from improper soil and nutrient management. Management of soil fertility is one of the challenging problem in the maize belt region of Nigeria because the soils are generally characterized by low nutrient status caused by the sandy nature of the soils [27], low use of organic and inorganic fertilizers [28], the impact of soil erosion caused by water [29], and absence of site-speciﬁc nutrient management guide [30]. This practice involves decreased soil disturbance, maintaining at least 30% permanent soil cover, and crop diversification (i.e., rotating/intercropping beans with other crops). 1. Decreasing soil disturbance: As summarized in Section 1.3.2, land can be prepared through ripping instead of ploughing while weeds can be uprooted or lightly scratched. Environmentally friendly herbicides can also be (responsibly) used to prevent harm to essential soil organisms and pollinator insects, and contamination of water bodies. Use of crop residue mulch: Mulching regulates soil temperature and surface-water flow after rains by encouraging infiltration of rainwater. Crop diversification: Rotate/intercrop beans with cereal or tuber crops rather than using continuous monocropping to avoid a build-up of pests and diseases. Common bean has been reported to increase yield of the cereal main crop by 10% and 20% under intercropping and rotational systems, respectively. [2] (Soil fertility management in Babati: A practical guide on good agricul, p.34) Utilizing locally available crops to improve soil fertility Intercropping such as maize and pigeon pea improves soil nutrient content and overall crop yields. However, rotations (even of intercropping systems) breaks pest and disease cycles. Exercise intercropping of cereals and legumes, and rotations, to achieve these benefits. The disease thrives in cool to moderate temperatures with extended periods of high relative humidity of more than 95%. Women often contribute substantially to household food security and natural-resource management but have limited access to land, production assets and formal markets. Grass seed banks and hay enterprises provide an opportunity to link rangeland restoration with local economic development. Water bunds complement this model by retaining runoff and improving moisture availability around grass establishment sites. In addition, Cd, Cr, Hg, Cu, Pb, and Ni are elements commonly found in sewage sludge, their presence and concentration depending on their source and sewage treatment procedures. Nevertheless, there is growing evidence that addressing the challenges of climate change, food and nutritional insecurity, and biodiversity loss is best accomplished within the framework of One Health. Integrated Pest Management (IPM), a concept that encompasses multiple pest control strategies, can be integrated into the One Health approach [12]. Historically, the application of IPM has demonstrated its multifaceted nature. For instance, biological control agents such as parasitoids and predators have been employed alongside habitat management tech­ niques like intercropping and the use of cover crops to enhance ecosystem services. These practices are often coupled with cultural ad­ justments, such as altering planting dates to disrupt pest life cycles, and mechanical methods like pheromone traps to monitor and reduce pest populations. Chemical controls, when used, are carefully integrated as a last resort, targeting specific pests with minimal non-target effects. Ex­ amples such as the push-pull strategy for controlling stemborers in maize fields [3], and the use of natural predators like Trichogramma wasps to manage caterpillar pests illustrate the inherently collaborative and adaptive framework of IPM. The strength of IPM lies in its dynamic, systems-based approach, which not only addresses the immediate challenges of pest control but also aligns with broader goals such as biodiversity conservation, soil health, and climate resilience. Therefore, this manuscript builds upon IPM’s foundational principles by proposing its integration into the Climate-Smart One Health (CS-OH) framework, emphasizing adaptability to climate variability and a focus on inter­ connected human, animal, plant, and environmental health. This inte­ grated perspective provides a path forward for enhancing IPM’s role in addressing the complex challenges posed by climate change and increasing agricultural sustainability [13,14].

Other water conservation structures include retention ditches and infiltration pits that collect and retain runoff water until it slowly seeps into the soil. The two structures are ideal for bean fields in dry areas where wet seasons are followed by prolonged dry spells. Otherwise, use cut-off drains to divert surface runoff from bean fields into appropriate drainage channels if your area receives more rainfall than can support bean growth.

Activity: mapping CSA practices under the three pillars Participants identified practices already known or used locally and discussed how each contributes to productivity, adaptation and mitigation. Examples included Bokashi/compost made from locally available materials such as ash, cow dung, charcoal and maize husks; biochar produced from maize, cotton and soya stalks; grass strips for erosion and runoff control; ripping under conservation farming; crop rotation; mulching; agroforestry; drainage; water harvesting; small-scale irrigation using treadle/chova or solar pumps; and improved or drought-tolerant varieties. The mapping exercise helped participants distinguish between simply listing technologies and assessing why a practice is suitable. For example, mulching can conserve soil moisture and reduce heat exposure at the soil surface; compost and Bokashi can support soil fertility and productivity; and agroforestry can contribute to resilience, soil protection and carbon storage. Participants noted that locally available materials are especially important where farmers face financial constraints.

Cultivating beans and other crops on the same piece of land facilitates the exploitation of nutrients from different soil layers at different times, thus preventing nutrient mining. Living organisms are also able to derive food from diverse plant sources. Crop diversity provides food and habitat for insects and could decrease pest attacks on beans while simultaneously enhancing pollination. You can maximize biodiversity through the following methods: ▶ Crop rotation: Cereal crops such as sorghum and maize or tubers such as cassava and potatoes are planted in one season and rotated with beans in subsequent seasons. ▶ Intercropping: A row of a cereal or tuber crop is alternated with beans on the same land and in the same season. ▶ Agroforestry: raising crops such as beans and trees on the same farm.
